question.problem: What is the length of the side opposite the ${30}^{∘}$ angle in a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle if the side opposite the ${60}^{∘}$ angle has a length of $21?$
question.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14185522/assets/1f7084b210e13a9c2753c3ae8bfcc9302b109cc9584f589c6b8937536ae93682.png)

  

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $21,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}21 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
x=\frac{21}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{21\sqrt{3}}{3}=7\sqrt{3}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $7\sqrt{3}.$
